newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Ombudsman appeals telecom rate changes.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Ombudsman appeals telecom rate changes.

text.p: Argentina's Ombudsman lodged a formal request Tuesday with a federal judge for recent changes to telephone charges to be reversed, the Ombudsman's office said.
"The measure is based on the unreasonableness of the changes to the tariff structure and the illegitimacy of the norms allowing such a procedure," Ombudsman Jorge Maiorano's office said.
The Ombudsman, who is appointed by Congress to defend citizens' rights, wants the judge to declare last Friday's decree authorizing the tariff changes unconstitutional.

Shares in Telefonica de Argentina and Telecom de Argentina rose sharply last week ater the government approved increases in local call charges and telephone rentals, as well as big reductions in long-distance rates.
"The court action does not question the reductions to the urban and interurban rates," the Ombudsman's office said.

Telefonica and Telecom had waged a long lobbying campaign for the tariff changes, which they said could make charges fairer for business and help them become more competitive by the time the Argentine phone market is thrown open to all competitors, probably in the year 2000.

But consumer groups and opposition parties fought hard against them, and argued in public hearings ending in December 1996 that private users' telephone bills would rise and the phone companies would pocket the difference.
Telecom stressed that there "was no way the rebalancing would mean higher earnings for the companies".

The changes abolish free local call time, boost the price of other local calls, and increase monthly rental charges. But the cost of the longest distance domestic calls has fallen by 56 percent and international call rates to major destinations have been cut by an average 42 percent.

Telecom is controlled by France Telecom, and Telefonica by Telefonica de Espana. The government granted them each near monopolies in territories which divided up Argentina between them when the former state telephone company ENTEL was privatized in 1990.
